name: Oman
summary: An Arabian sea power ruled by the Al Said dynasty since 1744; once held Zanzibar and the Swahili coast; modernised under Sultan Qaboos (1970–2020).

terrain.value: The Hajar Mountains, a coastal plain along the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, and the great desert of the interior.

climate.value: Hot and dry, with a southern monsoon (khareef) that brings mist and rain to Dhofar from June to September.

resources.value: Oil, natural gas, copper, fish, dates and frankincense.

disasters.value: Cyclone Gonu (2007) and Cyclone Shaheen (2021) caused floods and damage.

population.value: About 5.4 million (2026 estimate); 4.47 million at the 2020 census.

urbanisation.value: Muscat is the capital and largest city; Salalah, Sohar and Nizwa are other main towns.

disease.value: Health care has improved greatly since 1970, when there were almost no hospitals.

migration.value: Large numbers of foreign workers live in Oman, and many Omanis have ties to Zanzibar and East Africa.

economicBase.value: Oil and gas: 30.1% of GDP (2017), 71% of government revenue (2018) and 82.2% of product exports (2018). Fishing is not mentioned in the part read.

tradeRoutes.value: Zanzibar, the main slave market of the Swahili Coast and a major producer of cloves, was a valuable part of the Omani empire.

wealth.value: A high-income economy, based mainly on oil and gas.

moneyAndTax.value: The Omani rial, one of the highest-valued currencies; income tax is low.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy. Qaboos bin Said ruled 1970–2020; Haitham bin Tariq succeeded him.

keyRulers.value: Ahmad bin Said. Said bin Sultan. Qaboos bin Said.

succession.value: The Al Said dynasty has ruled since 1744; Qaboos took over from his father in 1970 and named no son as heir, and a successor was chosen from the family in 2020.

institutions.value: The Council of Oman, made up of an appointed State Council and an elected Consultative Council.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A navy and army built up with British help in the 1970s.

territoryChange.value: Zanzibar and the East African coast split off as a separate sultanate in 1861.

alliancesRivals.value: Close to Britain, and a neutral mediator that has hosted talks between Iran, the United States and others.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Few schools existed before 1970; Sultan Qaboos University opened in 1986.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Ships carried most trade; modern paved roads and airports were built after 1970.

languageWriting.value: Arabic, with some people speaking Balochi, Swahili and Mehri.

artsArchitecture.value: Great forts such as Nizwa and Bahla, mosques with domes and the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque in Muscat (2001).

socialStructure.value: Arabs, Baluchis and people of Swahili descent.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Omani identity based on seafaring, the Ibadi tradition and the Al Said monarchy.

dailyLife.value: Many families eat shuwa (slow-cooked marinated meat) at festivals, and drink Arabic coffee with dates.

neighbours.value: UAE, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Iran across the strait.

ideasReligions.value: Ibadi Islam, a distinct branch practised by about half of Omanis, is known for its tolerance.

colonisation.value: Portuguese held Muscat (1507–1650); later British influence.

riseSignals.value: The Al Bu Said dynasty came to power in 1744 and has ruled Oman ever since.

peakPeriod.value: At its 19th-century peak, Omani control reached across the Strait of Hormuz and south to Zanzibar, which became the empire’s capital in 1837.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
